opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few things that matter a lot, and they're somewhat different from what people might expect.

For research engineers, the most important thing is honestly just being very good at writing code quickly and reliably. A lot of our work is empirical. We build evaluations, we run models through lots of different scenarios, we build infrastructure to look at transcripts at scale. So someone who can take a vague idea and turn it into a working pipeline in a day or two, rather than in two weeks, is incredibly valuable. Speed of iteration is probably the single biggest predictor of how much progress a team makes. And I'd say software engineering experience from industry often transfers really well. You don't necessarily need an ML PhD for this.

For research scientists, I think the key skill is research taste, and that's a bit harder to pin down. It's about knowing which questions are worth asking, which experiments will actually update you, and when to stop pursuing something that isn't working. A lot of people early in their careers will run an experiment, get a result, and then not really know what it means or what to do next. Good researchers design experiments where they know in advance what they'd conclude from each possible outcome.

Then there are some things that cut across both roles. One is skepticism toward your own results. In evals especially, it's very easy to fool yourself. You see a model do something that looks like scheming, and you get excited. But then it turns out the prompt was leading, or there was a bug, or the model was just confused. So we really value people who instinctively try to break their own findings before anyone else does.

Another is actually reading the transcripts. That sounds trivial, but a surprising number of people look only at aggregate numbers. In our work you really need to look at what the model is saying and doing, because that's where you notice the weird stuff and form hypotheses.

And lastly, I'd say communication and a sense of ownership. We're a fairly small organization, so people need to be able to take a project, drive it forward somewhat independently, and then explain clearly what they found and how confident they are. Being calibrated about uncertainty, and writing it down clearly, matters a lot, especially because some of our findings end up informing labs and policymakers.

r001.rationale: The response describes Apollo’s work as empirical and explicitly values quick, reliable implementation and fast iteration.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that we care less about any specific technical skill and more about a handful of things that are harder to teach.

The first one is just taking the problem seriously in a fairly concrete way. A lot of people come in with a very abstract picture of AI safety, and what we actually want is someone who, when they sit down with a model, is asking: what would this system actually do in this specific situation, and how would I find out? So a kind of empirical mindset. You form a hypothesis, you go test it, you're willing to be wrong, and you update quickly. The people who've done well at Apollo are the ones who, when an experiment doesn't give them what they expected, get curious rather than frustrated.

The second is what I'd call research taste, which sounds vague, but it's basically the ability to pick the right question. There are a thousand things you could study about deceptive behavior or scheming in models, and most of them don't matter very much. Being able to say "this is the experiment that would actually change what we believe" is a big deal, and it's probably the main thing that separates people who are productive from people who are just busy. We try to assess that in interviews by giving people a somewhat open problem and seeing how they narrow it down.

Then on the engineering side — and this applies to the scientists too, honestly — being able to move fast and ship things. A lot of our evaluations work is quite practical. You need to build a harness, run a model through a bunch of scenarios, wrangle the outputs, and get a result by the end of the week, not the end of the quarter. So people who have a strong bias toward just getting something working and iterating are extremely valuable. For the engineers specifically, we care about being comfortable with large language model infrastructure, APIs, running things at scale, and being pretty rigorous about things like not accidentally leaking test information into your prompts, because those mistakes can quietly invalidate months of work.

And then the last one, which I think people underrate, is communication. If you find something concerning in a model, that's only useful if you can explain it clearly to a lab, to a policymaker, or in a paper, and explain exactly how confident you are and why. A result that nobody can interpret doesn't move the field. So we look for people who can write and who can say "here's what we know, here's what we don't, here's what I'd want to see next."

If I had to compress all of that, I'd say: curiosity about what models actually do, good judgment about which questions matter, the ability to execute quickly, and the honesty to communicate uncertainty. Specific skills — ML background, interpretability, whatever — we can usually help people pick up. Those other things are much harder to fake.

r001.rationale: The response values an empirical mindset—forming and testing hypotheses, updating quickly, and moving fast through practical experiments.

astra-6.text:
For research scientists, I think the most important thing is research taste: can you identify a question that matters, turn it into something you can actually test, and design an experiment where the result changes your mind? A lot of the work is quite ambiguous. You don’t necessarily have a well-defined problem and a standard method for solving it. You have to provide that structure yourself.

For research engineers, I’d put more weight on strong engineering skills and the ability to iterate quickly. Can you take an idea, implement it reliably, and notice when the experiment isn’t measuring what we thought it was measuring? There’s quite a lot of overlap between the roles. Ideally, engineers contribute to the research direction, and scientists can get their hands dirty with the implementation.

Across both, I really value intellectual honesty and ownership. If something doesn’t work, I want us to find that out, rather than produce a compelling story about why it worked. And I want people who will notice a problem and take responsibility for figuring it out, while being comfortable asking for help.

r001.rationale: The response values designing testable experiments and explicitly says research engineers should iterate quickly, communicating fast, iterative empirical research across the roles.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention AI scheming or translating it into an evaluation or model organism.

sol-6.1.text:
For research scientists, I think the biggest thing is research taste: can you identify the questions that actually matter, and then turn a fairly vague concern into an experiment that teaches us something? In our case, you might start with a concern about models being deceptive. But what precisely do you mean by deception? What would count as evidence for it? What alternative explanations do you need to rule out?

And then you need to be quite empirical. You should be willing to get your hands dirty, run experiments, look at what the model actually does, and change your mind when the results don’t fit your story. I value people who can move between the conceptual question and the concrete implementation.

For research engineers, strong software engineering skills are obviously important, but the research part matters too. You’re often building something where we don’t yet know exactly what the final experiment should look like. So you need judgment about what to make robust, what to prototype quickly, and when to flag that an experimental setup isn’t really measuring what we think it is.

Across both roles, I really value independence and good epistemics: people who take ownership, communicate uncertainty clearly, and are interested in finding out what’s true.

r001.rationale: The response values empirical work, running experiments, and changing course based on results; it also explicitly values prototyping quickly. Together these communicate fast, iterative empirical research.

r002.rationale: The response describes turning a concern about model deception into a concrete experiment by defining deception, specifying evidence, and ruling out alternatives. This communicates translating a form of scheming into an evaluation.
